question: How can tabular foundation models generalize across unrelated domains, what properties make pre-training tables useful, and should corpus design be understood in terms of datasets, examples, or the feature-target tasks induced during self-supervised pre-training?

key_findings.claim: Strong tabular in-context transfer can emerge from self-supervised pre-training on one real table, and tables that transfer well tend to be broadly useful across downstream datasets rather than useful only within their domain.
key_findings.evidence: The authors trained 88 separate TabDPT-style models on 88 real tables and evaluated each on 107 disjoint CC-18 and CTR-23 datasets. Rankings of pre-training tables were highly correlated across evaluation datasets, while the domain-to-domain rank matrix showed no same-domain advantage.

key_findings.claim: Feature count predicts single-table transfer much better than row count because randomized target and feature selection creates a combinatorial pool of training tasks.
key_findings.evidence: An XGBoost meta-model built from table statistics achieved R-squared 0.67 for average transfer performance, with feature count dominating importance and instance count negligible. On COLLEGES, removing about 70% of features reduced performance toward linear regression, while removing more than 70% of rows retained near-random-forest performance.

key_findings.claim: The number of distinct feature-target tasks, not raw table bytes or examples, is the main driver of broad transfer in the single-table regime.
key_findings.evidence: Holding rows and columns fixed while increasing the allowed task configurations from five to tens of thousands drove downstream AUC from near random, 0.5, to strong performance across tables. Adding a weak table to a strong one did not hurt: COLLEGES plus ANALCATDATA_SUPREME and APSFAILURE plus POKER-HAND both reached 0.919 AUC.

key_findings.claim: For large real-data corpora, coarse dataset filtering and exact deduplication do not help, whereas column-level cleaning consistently improves task quality without discarding whole task pools.
key_findings.evidence: On 1,732 OpenML tables, exact dataset deduplication changed average IQM from 0.9039 to 0.9038. Filtering to tables with at least 30 features reduced it to 0.8927. Column-level missingness removal, correlation deduplication, and minimum-feature enforcement produced regression R-squared IQM gains from +0.002 to +0.014; the best average reported was 0.9097.

key_findings.claim: The evidence supports a learned retrieval-and-aggregation account of tabular in-context learning more directly than a strict prior-fitting account.
key_findings.evidence: Across the 88 single-table models, exact-copy retrieval AUC correlated 0.89 with ordinary held-out CC-18 AUC. Forcing query and key projections to be shared, making attention a symmetric similarity rule, improved three weak-table models by +0.1088 AUC on average, cost only -0.0027 on three strong tables, and changed full-corpus AUC by +0.0001. Strong-model attention patterns were also more similar, with pair performance-similarity Spearman correlation 0.537.

method.core_idea: Hold the tabular ICL architecture and training recipe fixed, vary pre-training tables and task samplers, and connect transfer quality to the ability to retrieve and aggregate labeled context examples.
method.mechanism: Each pre-training task selects one table column as target and a subset of remaining columns as features. The study trains one model per real table, meta-regresses transfer on table properties, limits the number of unique task configurations, then scales to a 1,732-table OpenML corpus with dataset-level and column-level ablations. Mechanistic tests repeat context rows as queries, impose shared query-key projections so attention becomes a symmetric distance, and compare attention maps across independently trained models.
assumptions: The TabPFNv1/TabDPT row-based backbone and TabDPT-style task sampler are representative of modern tabular ICL.
Average accuracy and correlation across CC-18 and CTR-23 are adequate summaries of single-table transfer.
Exact-copy retrieval and attention similarity are informative proxies for the mechanisms supporting ordinary generalization.
Removing evaluation datasets from the pre-training corpus sufficiently separates pre-training and downstream tasks.
A randomized feature-target configuration is a meaningful unit of task diversity even when configurations are statistically dependent.

techniques.role: Isolates pre-training-table quality by training the same model independently on 88 real datasets.
Varies allowed feature-target configurations while preserving the source table's rows and columns.
Predicts average transfer from feature count, row count, data types, missingness, and training loss.
Removes mostly missing or highly correlated columns and skips only tables left with too few usable features.
Turns context points into identical queries to measure whether the model can recover their labels.
Constrains attention to a weighted inner-product distance, testing whether an explicit nearest-neighbor bias preserves transfer.
Tests whether independently trained high-performing models discover similar context-retrieval patterns.

evaluations.setting: 88 single-table pretrained models evaluated on 72 CC-18 classification and 35 CTR-23 regression datasets with no overlap.
evaluations.metric: Cross-task rankings and meta-model R-squared for average transfer.
evaluations.result: Training-table ranks were broadly correlated across tasks; a metadata XGBoost regressor achieved R-squared 0.67, led by feature count.
evaluations.baseline: The hypotheses that transfer is domain-specific or primarily controlled by number of rows.

evaluations.setting: Task-count intervention on fixed real tables.
evaluations.metric: Downstream CC-18 AUC as unique pre-training configurations increase.
evaluations.result: Performance rose consistently from near 0.5 with five tasks to strong AUC with tens of thousands of tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Five allowed feature-target task configurations under the same table size.

evaluations.setting: 1,732-table OpenML pre-training corpus evaluated on CC-18 and CTR-23; IQM with 95% intervals.
evaluations.metric: Average IQM over AUC, accuracy, correlation, and R-squared.
evaluations.result: Best listed average was 0.9097 with Pearson correlation deduplication plus minimum-five-feature enforcement; NaN plus Spearman plus minimum-five-feature scored 0.9091.
evaluations.baseline: Full-corpus average 0.9039; exact deduplication 0.9038; at-least-30-feature filtering 0.8927.

evaluations.setting: Larger model evaluated on 51 TabArena tasks at 1k, 2k, and 4k training contexts.
evaluations.metric: Pairwise task win rate of preprocessing versus matched unprocessed training.
evaluations.result: Preprocessing won 63% at 1k, 61% at 2k, and 67% at 4k; 4k plus preprocessing was strongest overall.
evaluations.baseline: Same larger architecture and context length without column preprocessing.

evaluations.setting: Mechanism probes on single-table models and the full OpenML corpus.
evaluations.metric: Retrieval-generalization Pearson correlation, AUC change under shared Q/K, and pair attention similarity.
evaluations.result: Retrieval versus ordinary AUC Pearson 0.89; shared Q/K gave +0.1088 on weak tables, -0.0027 on strong tables, and +0.0001 on the full corpus; pair performance-attention Spearman 0.537.
evaluations.baseline: Default independent query and key projections and independently trained weak-model attention patterns.

limitations: Author-stated: retrieval is not proven to be the only mechanism, and additional mechanisms cannot be definitively excluded.
Author-stated: experiments use real-data pre-training, so conclusions may not extend to models trained exclusively on synthetic priors.
Author-stated: the mechanism experiments use row-based attention and may not extend to cell-based tabular architectures.
Reviewer inference: exact-copy retrieval is easier than ordinary prediction and its correlation with AUC does not establish that the same attention operations cause downstream success.
Reviewer inference: the task-count intervention changes repeated exposure and sampler entropy together, so the independent contribution of task semantics is not fully isolated.
Reviewer inference: dataset-level deduplication is exact hash deduplication and does not test semantic or near-duplicate leakage.
failure_modes: A table with many redundant, missing, or nearly constant columns can have a large nominal task count but low effective task diversity.
Aggressive dataset filtering can discard simple dependency structures that complement feature-rich tables.
A symmetric nearest-neighbor bias can become restrictive when relevance is asymmetric, feature-dependent, or requires multi-step relational computation.
Retrieval can copy spurious near neighbors under distribution shift, class imbalance, or adversarial feature scaling.
A corpus can appear deduplicated by exact hashes while retaining transformed or semantically duplicate tables.
reusable_insights: Count distinct learnable relationships, not only examples or bytes, when designing in-context pre-training corpora.
Prefer feature-level task cleaning to whole-dataset exclusion when weak datasets add complementary structures.
Use retrieval probes and architectural constraints to test whether apparent foundation-model transfer is really a learned context algorithm.
Feature richness can create combinatorial supervision even when the source dataset is semantically narrow.
Strong cross-domain generalization need not imply broad parametric knowledge; it may reflect a domain-agnostic comparison and aggregation rule.
open_questions: What task-diversity statistic discounts redundant feature-target configurations and predicts transfer better than raw combinatorial count?
Can causal interventions on attention heads establish whether retrieval patterns cause tabular generalization?
How do the results change for cell-based models, synthetic-only priors, mixed real-synthetic curricula, and semantic column encoders?
When does asymmetric attention materially outperform symmetric similarity-based retrieval?
Can corpus sampling optimize marginal task novelty online without discarding useful low-feature tables?

competitive_landscape.title: TabPFN: A Transformer That Solves Small Tabular Classification Problems in a Second
competitive_landscape.difference: TabPFN trains on a broad synthetic structural-causal prior and interprets inference as approximate Bayesian prediction; this paper shows transfer from one unrelated real table and argues that learned retrieval and aggregation is a more parsimonious mechanism in that regime.

competitive_landscape.title: TabICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for In-Context Learning on Large Data
competitive_landscape.difference: TabICL scales synthetic pre-training and introduces a column-then-row architecture for very large tables; this paper fixes a row-based backbone and studies why even extremely narrow real-data pre-training can teach a transferable context algorithm.

competitive_landscape.title: Real-TabPFN: Improving Tabular Foundation Models via Continued Pre-training With Real-World Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Real-TabPFN reports that continued training on a small curated set of large real tables beats broader noisier corpora; this paper performs systematic single-table and corpus interventions and concludes that feature-target task count and column-level quality matter more than coarse dataset selection.

competitive_landscape.title: TabDPT-Turbo: Efficient In-Context Learning for Tabular Prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: TabDPT-Turbo targets efficient tabular in-context prediction on a large real-data corpus; this paper uses the TabDPT-style task construction as a controlled object and focuses on corpus mechanisms, single-table transfer, and retrieval rather than throughput.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: TabPFN established synthetic-prior ICL, TabICL scaled architecture and data, and Real-TabPFN established the value of curated real-data continuation. This paper's new contribution is the combination of a surprising single-table regime, evidence that feature-target task diversity dominates rows, practical column-level corpus rules, and three retrieval-oriented mechanism probes. The retrieval account is persuasive but not definitive because the evidence is correlational or based on a deliberately restricted attention intervention.
reviewer_notes: The main text and experimental sections were read in full. Numeric claims were checked on pages 3-10 and against Table 1. The TabPFN, TabICL, and Real-TabPFN comparisons were verified on primary arXiv pages; the TabDPT-Turbo identifier and title were cross-checked against the paper's primary arXiv citation.
